title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026
official_title: Streamlining Procurement for Effective Execution and Delivery and National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026
summary: Sets fiscal year 2026 policy and authorizations for the Department of Defense, military construction, and the Department of Energy's national security programs, with funding tables authorizing about $881.85B in total (the sum of the seven table titles). It also folds in the SPEED Act acquisition overhaul, bars the Federal Reserve from issuing a central bank digital currency, and reauthorizes the Coast Guard through 2029.
brief: Authorizes about $881.85B in fiscal year 2026 national defense programs and sets defense policy across six divisions, including a major acquisition-system overhaul.

top_lines.headline: Division A — Defense Authorizations
subs: Sets FY2026 DoD policy and end strengths (1,302,800 active-duty)
Bars DoD diversity, equity, and inclusion offices; merit-only personnel actions
Golden Dome missile-defense program and an ICBM floor of 400

top_lines.headline: Division B — Military Construction
subs: Itemized construction projects sum to about $15.08B
Base-housing reforms: mold, radon, and independent inspections
Renames two Georgia Army bases; single-sex facility rule on installations

top_lines.headline: Division C — DOE Nuclear and Maritime
subs: Plutonium pit floors: 30/yr at Los Alamos, 50/yr at Savannah River
New rapid program to develop modified nuclear weapons
$1.65B Maritime Administration; Chinese port-crane replacement

top_lines.headline: Division D — Funding Tables
subs: $295.08B operation and maintenance; $181.05B military personnel
$153.23B procurement; $142.44B research and development
$33.64B Department of Energy atomic-energy defense activities

top_lines.headline: Division E — Federal Reserve CBDC Ban
subs: Bars the Federal Reserve from issuing a central bank digital currency
Prohibits Fed retail accounts or products for individuals

top_lines.headline: Division F — Coast Guard Reauthorization
subs: Reauthorizes Coast Guard appropriations through FY2029
Main appropriation line rises to $15.50B by FY2029

likelihoodReason: Passed the House on September 30, 2025 and received in the Senate; sponsored by a majority-party member (R-AL) with the House under Republican control. As the House's annual defense authorization vehicle it is positioned to advance, but the Senate typically passes its own National Defense Authorization Act and reconciles the two in conference, so the enacted text will differ from this House version. The acquisition-threshold increases, the diversity-office prohibitions, and the central bank digital currency ban are the provisions most likely to draw Senate changes.

items.main: Authorizes fiscal year 2026 procurement appropriations for the Army, the Navy and Marine Corps, the Air Force and Space Force, and Defense-wide activities, with amounts set by the funding table in section 4101.
items.detail: Section 101 states no aggregate dollar figure in this text; the amounts are cross-referenced to the section 4101 funding table located in division D. Subtitles B through E add program-specific procurement authorities, limitations, and reporting requirements.

items.main: Grants contract authority for up to two Ford class aircraft carriers and up to five Columbia class submarines, plus advance procurement of Virginia class submarine components and multiyear UH-60 Blackhawk procurement.
items.detail: Contracts may use incremental funding, with government termination liability limited to funds obligated at the time of termination. Multiyear UH-60 Blackhawk procurement begins with the fiscal year 2027 program year; yard, repair, berthing, and messing barge multiyear procurement begins in fiscal year 2026.

items.main: Raises the air-refueling tanker inventory floor from 466 to 485 aircraft (from Oct 1, 2026) and to 504 (from Oct 1, 2027), bars A-10 retirements through Sep 30, 2026 with a 162-aircraft floor, and extends the B-1 bomber squadron reduction ban to Sep 30, 2030.
items.detail: The Department may not accept KC-46 aircraft beyond 183 until it certifies a plan to resolve all Category 1 deficiencies. Retired KC-10 aircraft must be preserved in flyable condition while the tanker inventory is below 504. The prohibition on foreign-made light detection and ranging technology is expanded.

sections.label: Title II — Research, Development, Test, and Evaluation

items.main: Authorizes fiscal year 2026 research, development, test, and evaluation appropriations per the section 4201 funding table, with numerous line-item increases each offset by an equal operation-and-maintenance reduction.
items.detail: No aggregate dollar figure appears in this text. The largest specified increase is $50M for a Navy quantum communications corridor, offset by a $50M reduction to Army operation and maintenance; other specified increases range from $3M to $10M.

items.main: Authorizes a National Security and Defense Artificial Intelligence Institute and a ten-year initiative to assess advanced artificial intelligence and the People's Republic of China's artificial-intelligence progress for national security.
items.detail: The Institute awards five-year financial assistance, renewable once, only to institutions of higher education based in the United States. The strategic-competition initiative reports to Congress every 180 days and sunsets after ten years. A Biotechnology Supply Chain Resiliency Program is also authorized with a ten-year sunset.

items.main: Imposes a three-year post-employment bar on Department of Defense principal investigators and laboratory employees accepting compensation from a foreign entity of concern, and raises the advanced-technology prize cap.
items.detail: The prize competition congressional-notification threshold is raised from $10M to $20M, and the maximum prize is set at $20M without Secretary of Defense approval. The title also prohibits fiscal year 2026 funds for gain-of-function research on potential pandemic pathogens (waivable) and for animal research conducted with a foreign country of concern.

items.main: Authorizes fiscal year 2026 operation and maintenance appropriations per the section 4301 funding table; no aggregate dollar figure appears in this text.
items.detail: One specified line-item change adds $35M for Army Reserve Expeditionary Combat Aviation Brigade flight hours, offset by a $35M reduction to Army-Servicewide Transportation.

items.main: Directs a Department executive agent, an interagency working group, and pilot programs to pursue nuclear reactors at military installations, and expands per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances investigation, remediation, and alternative-drinking-water requirements.
items.detail: Nuclear energy and nuclear technologies are added to the Office of Strategic Capital's eligible investments. Households with private wells contaminated above the maximum contaminant level by Department activity must be provided an alternative drinking-water source. The fluorinated aqueous film-forming foam replacement deadline moves from Oct 1, 2023 to Oct 1, 2026, and the trigger is lowered from 'in excess of one part per billion' to 'detectable'.

items.main: Eliminates the Department of Defense preference for electric or hybrid motor vehicles and repeals related requirements, and establishes statutory Army and Navy museum systems and a National Guard study center.
items.detail: Section 324 strikes 10 U.S.C. 2922g and paragraphs of section 2911(e). New statutory sections create the Army Museum System, the United States Navy Museum System, and the Center for the Study of the National Guard. Military rotary-wing training in highly trafficked domestic airspace must provide warnings compatible with the traffic alert and collision avoidance system of nearby commercial aircraft.

items.main: Sets fiscal year 2026 active-duty end strengths as of Sep 30, 2026 totaling 1,302,800: Army 454,000, Navy 344,600, Marine Corps 172,300, Air Force 321,500, and Space Force 10,400.
items.detail: The total is the sum of the five component figures stated in section 401. Each figure is the authorized active-duty strength as of the last day of fiscal year 2026.

items.main: Sets Selected Reserve end strengths as of Sep 30, 2026 totaling 773,400 across seven components, ranging from 328,000 (Army National Guard) to 8,500 (Coast Guard Reserve).
items.detail: The total is the sum of the seven component figures in section 411. The title also caps full-time reserve support personnel and reserve members on operational-support active duty, and sets dual-status military technician minimums, including 21,294 for the Army National Guard.

items.main: Authorizes fiscal year 2026 military personnel appropriations per the section 4401 funding table and streamlines force-reporting requirements.
items.detail: The military personnel authorization supersedes any other fiscal year 2026 authorization for that purpose. The annual report on military technicians is repealed, and the civilian personnel management report is folded into the annual Defense Manpower Profile Report. National Guard members on duty supporting military intelligence operations are excluded from active-duty end-strength counts.

items.main: All DoD military personnel actions must be based exclusively on individual merit, and consideration of race, ethnicity, or national origin is prohibited (Sec 524).
items.detail: Section 524 requires accessions, promotions, assignments, command selection, and schooling selection to rest on merit, fitness, capability, and performance, with a limited exception for tasking specific unconventional foreign missions that requires combatant-commander approval and a report within 60 days. Section 525 bars using any funds authorized by the Act for diversity, equity, and inclusion, and Section 526 bars issuing a new COVID-19 vaccine mandate to replace the one rescinded in the FY2023 NDAA.

items.main: Every male citizen and male resident aged 18 to 26 is automatically registered by the Selective Service System (Sec 534).
items.detail: Section 534 replaces self-registration with automatic registration by the Director, who may collect date of birth, address, Social Security number, phone, and email, and must notify each registrant. Aliens holding lawful nonimmigrant status are excluded while that status is maintained, and the change takes effect one year after enactment.

items.main: Creates a new UCMJ article for child pornography with tiered penalties and authorizes the death penalty for rape of a child (Sec 553-554).
items.detail: Section 553 adds article 117b setting maximum confinement of 10 years for possessing, receiving, or viewing; 15 years for possession with intent to distribute; 20 years for distribution; and 30 years for production, each with dishonorable discharge and forfeiture of all pay and allowances. Section 552 rewrites the intimate-images offense to cover digital forgeries (deepfakes), and Section 554 makes rape of a child punishable by death.

sections.label: Title VI — Compensation and Other Personnel Benefits

items.main: Extends expiring bonus and special pay authorities one year, from Dec 31, 2025 to Dec 31, 2026 (Sec 611).
items.detail: Section 611 pushes back the sunset on general enlisted and officer bonus authorities, aviation and nuclear-officer incentive pay, health-professional accession and loan-repayment authorities, hazardous-duty and assignment pay, and the temporary BAH-increase authority. Each affected provision changes 'December 31, 2025' to 'December 31, 2026.'

items.main: Establishes explosive ordnance disposal incentive pay of $125 to $1,000 per month (Sec 612).
items.detail: Section 612 adds section 301f to title 37, giving members with an EOD designator continuous monthly incentive pay scaled by years of EOD duty, from $125 at two years or fewer up to $1,000 over 10 years, then declining to $250 over 25 years. It takes effect 180 days after enactment, and reserve members receive one-thirtieth of the monthly rate per day of EOD duty performed under orders.

items.main: Sets the family separation allowance at a flat $400 and lowers the BAH increase trigger to a 15 percent cost gap (Sec 622, 626).
items.detail: Section 622 replaces the $250-to-$400 range with a fixed $400 monthly family separation allowance. Section 626 lowers the threshold for a temporary BAH increase from a 20 percent to a 15 percent housing-cost difference and strikes the provision's expiration, making the authority permanent.

items.main: Requires TRICARE Prime and TRICARE Select to cover fertility-related care for active-duty members and their dependents.
items.detail: New section 1074p of title 10 mandates the coverage; in vitro fertilization is limited to three completed oocyte retrievals per calendar year, with single embryo transfers unless otherwise medically indicated under American Society for Reproductive Medicine guidelines. Cost-sharing is set under existing TRICARE cost-share provisions, and former members are excluded.

items.main: Requires TRICARE to cover up to a 365-day supply of contraceptives in a single fill or refill.
items.detail: Beginning not less than 180 days after enactment, an eligible beneficiary may obtain up to a 365-day supply of a uniform-formulary contraceptive at the beneficiary's option, through a military treatment facility, retail, or mail-order pharmacy.

items.main: Bars TRICARE from covering or furnishing gender-related medical treatment, with specified exceptions.
items.detail: New section 1076g excludes gender-related medical treatment from care under section 1076 for members and dependents. Exceptions cover treatment for a diagnosed disorder of sex development or irresolvably ambiguous biological sex characteristics.

sections.label: Title VIII — Acquisition Policy, Acquisition Management, and Related Matters

items.main: Requires DoD to enter multiyear contracts for covered weapon systems projected to require more than $1B in procurement (FY2025 dollars).
items.detail: The mandate applies once a system reaches full-rate production and is projected to hold full-rate production for five or more consecutive years, subject to section 3501 of title 10. The Secretary of Defense may waive the requirement based on the projected threat environment.

items.main: Adds a 30-day price-spike reporting duty and shortens unit-cost (Nunn-McCurdy) breach reporting to Congress to within 30 days.
items.detail: New section 3709 requires an offeror to report within 30 days when a covered-contract price reaches or exceeds 25 percent above the bid price or 25 percent above the prior calendar year's price. Section 806 also designates end items projected above $500M as major subprograms for acquisition reporting.

items.main: Removes the Berry Amendment small-purchase exception and sets a $250,000 small-purchase exception for strategic and critical materials.
items.detail: Section 4862 is amended to strike its small-purchase exception and replace subsection (h) with a committee to oversee compliance. Section 4863 gains a $250,000 small-purchase exception for strategic materials, adjustable every five years for changes in the Consumer Price Index.

sections.label: Title IX — Department of Defense Organization and Management

items.main: Section 901 bars the Secretary of Defense from maintaining diversity, equity, inclusion, or accessibility offices, positions, training courses, affinity groups, and data dashboards.
items.detail: It repeals the Chief Diversity Officer (10 U.S.C. 147) and the Program on Diversity in Military Leadership (10 U.S.C. 656) and strikes diversity-and-inclusion reporting requirements from 10 U.S.C. 113. Equal Employment Opportunity offices and offices enforcing the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, as historically organized and operated within the Department, are preserved.

items.main: Section 912 establishes a Joint Counter-Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Office to validate and approve counter-drone systems before any component may procure them.
items.detail: The Office's Director reports to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and maintains the list of validated, approved systems; no component may buy a counter-drone system that is not on the list unless a service acquisition executive or the Under Secretary for Acquisition and Sustainment waives the restriction with notice to the congressional defense committees. The Director must submit an initial strategic plan within 120 days of standing up and file annual reports on activities and expenditures.

items.main: Section 911 adds the Commandant of the Coast Guard as a member of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and makes the Commandant eligible for appointment as Chairman.
items.detail: Conforming amendments to titles 10 and 14 extend Joint Staff membership to the Coast Guard and require the Commandant to keep the Secretary of the department in which the Coast Guard operates informed of military advice and significant operations. Section 919 further makes the Chief of the National Guard Bureau eligible for appointment as Chairman.

items.main: Section 1001 lets the Secretary of Defense transfer up to $6B among fiscal year 2026 defense authorizations when determined necessary in the national interest.
items.detail: Transfers may only fund items of higher priority and may not fund items Congress has denied; transfers between military personnel authorizations under title IV do not count toward the $6B cap. The Secretary must promptly notify Congress of each transfer.

items.main: Section 1008 cuts Department of Defense discretionary budget authority by .5 percent each fiscal year if it has not submitted a prior-year financial statement or obtained at least a qualified audit opinion.
items.detail: The reduction is applied on March 2, proportionally across accounts, and the cut amount is retained in the Treasury for deficit reduction. Military personnel, reserve, National Guard, and Defense Health Program accounts are excluded, and the President may waive the cut for an account to protect national security or deployed troops.

items.main: Sections 1032 through 1035 extend prohibitions on transferring Guantanamo Bay detainees to the United States or to certain countries, and on closing the facility, through December 31, 2026.
items.detail: Each provision strikes the prior December 31, 2025 (or fiscal year 2025) end date and substitutes the 2026 date. The prohibitions bar using funds to transfer or release detainees to the United States, construct facilities to house them, transfer them to certain countries, or relinquish control of the naval station.

items.main: Section 1111 lets Department of Defense element heads reprimand, suspend, reassign, demote, or remove Senior Executive Service career appointees for documented misconduct or performance, and remove them from the civil service.
items.detail: The notice-response-decision process is capped at 15 business days, with a 7-business-day employee response window and a separate grievance process of fewer than 21 days; appeals go to the Merit Systems Protection Board, which must decide within 120 days. The authority sunsets on September 30, 2030.

items.main: Section 1110 bars using fiscal year 2026 Department of Defense funds to implement Executive Order 14251 on excluding agencies from federal labor-management relations programs.
items.detail: The prohibition covers the March 27, 2025 order and any following policy or guidance. It applies to funds authorized or otherwise made available for the Department for fiscal year 2026.

items.main: Subtitle B, the Defense Hiring Modernization Act of 2025, lets the Department use skills-based hiring, structured assessments, shared talent pools, and promotions without time-in-grade minimums.
items.detail: Amendments to title 5 authorize competency-based qualification and assessment procedures, flexible outreach, and shared certificates of eligibles valid for at least one year, subject to Office of Personnel Management regulations and merit-system principles. The Secretary must report on hiring impact within one year.

sections.label: Title XII — Matters Relating to Foreign Nations

items.main: Raises the U.S.-Israel counter-unmanned-systems program authorization from $55M to $70M and extends it through Dec 31, 2028.
items.detail: Section 1213 broadens the program from 'unmanned aerial systems' to 'unmanned systems in all warfighting domains' and moves it to the Irregular Warfare Technology Support Directorate. Section 1212 extends U.S.-Israel anti-tunnel cooperation to Dec 31, 2028 and Section 1211 extends Israel war reserve stockpile authority to Jan 1, 2029.

items.main: Extends authorities for vetted Syrian groups, counter-ISIS assistance, and Lebanon counter-terrorism support through Dec 31, 2026, and bars FY2026 funds to the Badr Organization.
items.detail: Sections 1233-1235 extend the underlying FY2015 and FY2016 authorities by one year. Lebanon support under Section 1235 may be used only to counter Lebanese Hezbollah, Hamas, ISIS, and other terrorist groups; Section 1236 prohibits any FY2026 Defense funds to the Badr Organization.

items.main: Extends the annual military-power reports on Iran (to Dec 31, 2030), Russia (to Jan 31, 2030), and China (to Jan 31, 2030).
items.detail: Section 1238 expands the Iran report to cover proxies including Hezbollah, Hamas, Palestine Islamic Jihad, and Ansar Allah, plus Russian arms transfers to Iran. Section 1241 rewrites the Russia report and Section 1243 adds Taiwan-conflict cyber, blockade, and invasion scenarios to the China report.

sections.label: Title XIII — Other Matters Relating to Foreign Nations

items.main: Extends the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative through Dec 31, 2028 and authorizes $300M for FY2026 and $300M for FY2027.
items.detail: Section 1302 requires the President to submit a written determination that obligating the funds is in the U.S. national interest before any amounts for a fiscal year may be obligated or expended.

items.main: Bars using FY2026 funds to cut EUCOM forces below 76,000 or to return EUCOM sites until certifications are submitted; the limitation sunsets Sept 30, 2026.
items.detail: Section 1304 conditions any reduction on certifications covering national-security rationale, NATO consultation, and a Russia threat assessment. Section 1305 states NATO members should commit 3.5% of GDP to core defense and 1.5% to defense-related infrastructure; Section 1306 establishes a Baltic Security Initiative for Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania.

items.main: Authorizes up to $1B of FY2026 Defense funds for the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative and directs an invitation for Taiwan's navy to the Rim of the Pacific exercise.
items.detail: Section 1313 sets the $1B FY2026 cap; Section 1323 directs the RIMPAC invitation. Section 1316 states approximately 28,500 U.S. forces should remain in South Korea, and Section 1311 extends the Pacific Deterrence Initiative to FY2026.

items.main: Authorizes FY2026 appropriations for working-capital funds, chemical agents and munitions destruction, drug interdiction and counter-drug activities, the Defense Inspector General, and the Defense Health Program.
items.detail: No dollar figures appear in this title's text; amounts are set by the funding table in section 4501. Defense Health Program funds provide for the health of eligible beneficiaries; chemical destruction funds destroy lethal chemical agents under 50 U.S.C. 1521.

items.main: Authorizes up to $162.5M transfer to the Lovell Health Care Center fund and $77M from the Armed Forces Retirement Home Trust Fund for FY2026.
items.detail: Section 1411 extends the Lovell demonstration-fund authority to Sept 30, 2027. Section 1414 authorizes the $77M Armed Forces Retirement Home appropriation for its operation.

items.main: Amends National Defense Stockpile shortfall briefings and fixes Defense Logistics Agency Working Capital Fund audit opening balances.
items.detail: Section 1412 adds required briefing contents including the cost to remedy shortfalls and amounts appropriated. Section 1413 sets statutory opening ledger balances for the DLA Working Capital Fund for audit (Cumulative Results of Operations $27.27B); Section 1415 requires a rare-earth-element recovery report.

items.main: Establishes Authorization-to-Operate Expedited Appeals Boards DoD-wide and in each military department to decide cloud Authorization-to-Operate requests within 90 days.
items.detail: Section 1501 requires the boards within 180 days of enactment. Once a stakeholder appeals an Authorization to Operate that has been pending more than 180 days, the authorizing official loses authority to grant or deny it; biannual reports run through Oct 1, 2031.

items.main: Directs the Navy to require updated cyber protections in wireless-telecom contracts, including disabling 2G and 3G networks and defending against SS7 and Diameter attacks.
items.detail: Section 1513 also requires storing call data records no longer than 60 days, blocking forced 3G downgrades, and publishing quarterly independent cyber audits. The Navy must certify implementation within 180 days.

items.main: Requires a Department-wide AI and machine-learning cybersecurity policy, an AI software bill of materials, and 2 to 12 generative-AI efforts.
items.detail: Section 1531 addresses model tampering, data leakage, and adversarial prompt injection. Section 1533 directs not fewer than 2 and not more than 12 generative-AI efforts; Section 1515 requires a strategy against AI-enabled cyberattacks including deepfakes and voice cloning.

sections.label: Title XVI — Space Activities, Strategic Programs, and Intelligence Matters

items.main: Rewrites U.S. national missile-defense policy to deploy a next-generation missile-defense shield ('Golden Dome for America') and bars subscription-based or privatized intercept capabilities.
items.detail: Section 1641 amends 10 U.S.C. 5501 and Section 1642 requires a development-and-deployment plan within 180 days under Executive Order 14186. Section 1643 requires kinetic missile-defense systems be owned and operated by the armed forces; Section 1623 bars reducing deployed intercontinental ballistic missiles below 400.

items.main: Establishes Air Force Global Strike Command as a major command and creates a Space Force acquisition career path with a Senate-confirmed Program Executive Officer for Assured Access to Space.
items.detail: Section 1621 makes the Global Strike Command commander a four-star single accountable officer for the nuclear and long-range strike missions. Section 1601 requires at least 40% of Space Force officer-training graduates be assigned to acquisition or operational billets; Section 1608 authorizes Space Command to help track fentanyl trafficking.

items.main: Authorizes $282.8M for FY2026 Cooperative Threat Reduction and creates a clandestine-activities vendor database.
items.detail: Section 1651 allocates the CTR total, with $160.4M for biological threat reduction the largest line. Section 1611 requires a centralized database of vendors supporting clandestine Defense activities; Section 1616 bars DoD cloud access by citizens of foreign countries of concern.

items.main: Repeals the 1991 and 2002 Authorizations for Use of Military Force against Iraq.
items.detail: Section 1733F repeals the Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution (Public Law 102-1) and the Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution of 2002 (Public Law 107-243). Both are struck as notes to 50 U.S.C. 1541.

items.main: Bars military commissaries and exchanges from selling vape or oral-nicotine products without manufacturer FDA certification.
items.detail: Section 1702 requires manufacturers of ENDS products and oral nicotine products to certify under penalty of perjury an FDA marketing granted order, or a timely-filed premarket tobacco product application, before sale at any Defense Commissary Agency, Army and Air Force Exchange Service, Navy Exchange, or Marine Corps Exchange outlet. Each resale entity must publish a product directory within 180 days and recertify annually; uncertified products face removal, seizure, forfeiture, and destruction after a 30-day cure period.

items.main: Extends federal recognition to the Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina.
items.detail: Section 1733C amends the Act of June 7, 1956 to grant the Lumbee Tribe federal recognition and eligibility for all services the Federal Government provides to recognized tribes. Members residing in Robeson, Cumberland, Hoke, and Scotland counties are deemed to reside on or near a reservation, and the Secretary of the Interior is authorized to take land into trust for the tribe.

sections.label: Title XVIII — Streamlining Procurement for Effective Execution and Delivery

items.main: Raises major acquisition dollar thresholds, including the major defense acquisition program development threshold from $300M (FY1990) to $1B (FY2025).
items.detail: Section 1821 raises the major defense acquisition program thresholds to $1B for research and development and $4.5B for procurement (2024 dollars), the major program thresholds to $275M and $1.3B, the micro-purchase threshold from $10K to $25K, the simplified small-purchase threshold from $5M to $10M, and the certified cost-or-pricing data threshold from $2M to $10M. The approval thresholds for using procedures other than competitive procedures rise from $10M to $100M and from $75M to $500M.

items.main: Rewrites the objectives of the defense acquisition system and creates new requirements and engineering coordination bodies.
items.detail: Section 1801 rewrites 10 U.S.C. 3102 so the acquisition system exists to expeditiously provide the armed forces with needed capabilities in the most cost-effective manner, with guidance encouraging iterative development and learning through failure. Section 1811 renames the Joint Requirements Oversight Council the Joint Requirements Council; Section 1812 creates the Requirements, Acquisition, and Programming Integration Directorate (RAPID); and Section 1813 establishes a Mission Engineering and Integration Activity. Sections 1802 and 1803 add statutory program executive officer and product support manager roles.

items.main: Establishes the Defense Industrial Resilience Consortium and directs advanced-manufacturing transition and workforce reviews.
items.detail: Section 1842 directs the Secretary of Defense to establish, within 90 days, a Defense Industrial Resilience Consortium of government, industry, and academia to address supply-chain fragility, expand domestic manufacturing capacity, and develop the manufacturing workforce. Section 1835 requires each major weapon system program executive officer to plan transition of critical items to advanced manufacturing within 24 months, and Section 1843 sets up a consortium working group on qualifying and accepting advanced-manufactured products. Section 1841 raises the Procurement Technical Assistance Program funding cap from $1M to $1.5M.

items.main: $2.40B in Army construction and land acquisition across U.S. and overseas installations (sum of the Section 2101 project tables).
items.detail: Largest projects include $457M at Naval Air Station Key West, $440M at Joint Region Marianas (Guam), $208M at Fort Wainwright, and $196M at Joint Base Lewis-McChord. Overseas amounts ($154M) cover U.S. Army garrisons in Germany. Total project cost may not exceed the amount authorized in the section 4601 funding table.

items.main: $195.7M for Army family housing construction in Belgium and Germany, plus up to $33M for planning and design.
items.detail: Section 2102 authorizes family housing units at Chievres Air Base, Belgium ($145M) and U.S. Army Garrison Bavaria, Germany ($51M). Architectural, engineering, and construction design activities for family housing are capped at $33M.

items.main: Extends several prior-year Army project authorizations to October 1, 2026 and moves one fiscal year 2025 barracks project to a new location.
items.detail: Sections 2104-2106 keep fiscal year 2021-2023 authorizations in effect, including the Fort Gillem forensic laboratory ($71M) and Fort Stewart barracks ($105M). Section 2107 lets the Army build the fiscal year 2025 Hohenfels barracks at Smith Barracks, Germany instead.

items.main: $5.84B in Navy and Marine Corps construction, the division's largest service total (sum of the Section 2201 tables).
items.detail: Largest projects are $1.58B at Naval Station Norfolk and $1.04B at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard. Other large items include $430M at Naval Support Activity Monterey, $399.6M at Naval Air Station Lemoore, and $374.9M at Naval Air Station Jacksonville. One overseas project ($58M) is at Marine Corps Base Camp Smedley D. Butler, Japan.

items.main: Up to $68M to improve existing Navy family housing, plus up to $7M for planning and design.
items.detail: Section 2202 authorizes improvements to existing military family housing units under section 2825 of title 10, plus related architectural and engineering services, each capped at the stated amount.

items.main: Extends fiscal year 2022 and 2023 Navy and Marine Corps project authorizations to October 1, 2026.
items.detail: Sections 2204-2206 keep prior-year authorizations in effect, including Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point flightline utilities modernization ($113.5M) and Marine Corps Recruit Depot Parris Island recruit barracks.

sections.label: Title XXIII — Air Force Military Construction

items.main: $2.73B in Air Force and Space Force construction across U.S. and overseas bases (sum of the Section 2301 tables).
items.detail: Largest projects are $389M at Tinker Air Force Base, $378M at Ellsworth Air Force Base, $253M at Royal Air Force Lakenheath (United Kingdom), and $250M at Hill Air Force Base. Overseas projects total $450M, at sites in the United Kingdom, Germany, Greenland, Norway, and Diego Garcia.

items.main: Up to $237.7M to improve existing Air Force family housing, plus up to $37M for planning and design.
items.detail: Section 2302 authorizes improvements to existing family housing units under section 2825 of title 10 and related construction design services.

items.main: Extends fiscal year 2017-2023 Air Force project authorizations to October 1, 2026 and modifies a fiscal year 2025 Wyoming project.
items.detail: Sections 2304-2308 keep prior authorizations in effect. Section 2309 lets the Air Force build 3,219 kilometers of telephone duct facility for the Ground Based Strategic Deterrent Utility Corridor at F.E. Warren Air Force Base.

sections.label: Title XXIV — Defense Agencies Military Construction

items.main: $2.15B in defense-agency construction plus $684.3M in Energy Resilience and Conservation Investment Program (ERCIP) projects (sums of the Section 2401 and 2402 tables).
items.detail: Defense-agency construction includes $500M at a Texas site, $255M at Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune, $254.7M at Fort Bragg, and $397.5M at Royal Air Force Lakenheath. ERCIP funds microgrid and power projects, including $146.8M at Marine Corps Air Station Iwakuni, Japan and $124M at Cape Cod Space Force Station.

items.main: Modifies the fiscal year 2024 microgrid project at Lake City Army Ammunition Plant to $86.5M and adjusts other prior-year projects.
items.detail: Section 2408 revises the Lake City project scope (liquid propane gas tanks and related equipment) and amends its amount to $86.5M. Sections 2404-2410 extend or modify fiscal year 2019-2025 defense-agency and energy projects.

items.main: Authorizes U.S. contributions to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) Security Investment Program, with no dollar figure stated in the division text.
items.detail: Section 2501 lets the Secretary of Defense contribute the U.S. share of NATO construction, not to exceed the amount in the section 4601 funding table plus amounts NATO repays for construction previously financed by the United States.

items.main: Accepts $453M in Republic of Korea-funded and $504.2M in Republic of Poland-funded in-kind construction projects.
items.detail: Sections 2511-2512 let the Secretary of Defense accept host-nation-funded projects, including a $180M runway at Camp Humphreys (Korea) and a $199M barracks and dining facility at Powdiz (Poland). These projects are funded by the host nations, not by U.S. appropriations.

sections.label: Title XXVI — Guard and Reserve Forces Facilities

items.main: $685.2M for National Guard and Reserve construction across the components (sum of the Sections 2601-2605 tables).
items.detail: Includes $191.8M for Army National Guard, $168M for Army Reserve (Fort Knox $138M; New Castle $30M), $106.9M for Navy and Marine Corps Reserve at Naval Air Station Fort Worth, $200.5M for Air National Guard, and $18M for Air Force Reserve.

items.main: Authorizes a new fiscal year 2026 Army Reserve project at Conroe, Texas using prior-year funds, capped at $12M.
items.detail: Section 2609 authorizes a rotary-wing landing pad and taxiway at Army Reserve Center Conroe using unobligated funds appropriated before fiscal year 2026 under the 'Military Construction, Army Reserve' heading. Section 2607 extends fiscal year 2023 Guard and Reserve authorizations to October 1, 2026.

sections.label: Title XXVII — Base Realignment and Closure Activities

items.main: Authorizes appropriations for base realignment and closure (BRAC) activities through the Department of Defense Base Closure Account, with no dollar figure stated in the division text.
items.detail: Section 2701 authorizes real property acquisition and military construction under the Defense Base Closure and Realignment Act of 1990, funded through the Base Closure Account as specified in the section 4601 funding table.

sections.label: Title XXVIII — Military Construction General Provisions

items.main: Creates new construction authorities: transactions other than contracts, multiyear contracting, and additive-manufacturing and additive-construction pilots.
items.detail: Section 2801 adds title 10 Section 2808a for repair and construction via transactions other than contracts, cooperative agreements, or grants. Section 2807 allows fiscal year 2026 multiyear contracts for unaccompanied housing and child development centers if a 10 percent cost savings is certified. Sections 2805 and 2857 establish additive-construction and additive-manufacturing pilots.

items.main: Adds base-housing reforms covering mold, radon, home inspections, and waitlist reporting.
items.detail: Sections 2816-2818 create a mold-remediation pilot, joint mold-remediation guidelines, and independent inspections of privatized housing. Section 2820 requires radon testing against the Environmental Protection Agency action level, and a new title 10 Section 2840 requires an annual military family housing waitlist report.

items.main: Raises minor-construction spending limits, renames two Georgia Army bases, and authorizes land conveyances.
items.detail: Sections 2852-2854 raise unspecified minor military construction and defense-laboratory limits (including $150M to $300M for the Defense Laboratory Modernization Program). Sections 2833-2834 designate an Augusta, Georgia installation 'Fort Shugart Gordon' and a Muscogee and Chattahoochee County installation 'Fort Moore.' Sections 2842-2843 authorize conveyances of the former Curtis Bay Depot (about 435 acres) in Maryland and about 19 acres at Naval Air Station Key West.

sections.label: Title XXXI — Department of Energy National Security Programs

items.main: Authorizes FY2026 appropriations for National Nuclear Security Administration programs, defense environmental cleanup, other defense activities, and nuclear energy.
items.detail: Amounts are set by the funding table in section 4701, which is not included in this division text, so no dollar figures are stated here. Funds go to the Department of Energy for the listed fiscal year 2026 activities.

items.main: Requires minimum war reserve plutonium pit production of 30 per year at Los Alamos and 50 per year at Savannah River.
items.detail: Amends section 4219 of the Atomic Energy Defense Act to direct the Secretary of Energy to ensure Los Alamos National Laboratory (New Mexico) can reliably produce at least 30 pits annually and the Savannah River Plutonium Processing Facility (Aiken, South Carolina) at least 50 annually. No date to reach these capacities is stated in the text.

items.main: Creates a rapid capabilities program to develop new or modified nuclear weapons, targeting a first production unit within 5 years.
items.detail: Adds section 4225 to the Atomic Energy Defense Act, run by the Secretary of Energy through the Administrator in coordination with the Secretary of Defense. Objectives include reusing existing components, using tailored risk-acceptance processes, and limited production quantities; program amounts are to be identified in future budget justifications to Congress.

sections.label: Title XXXII — Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board

items.main: Authorizes $45M for FY2026 operation of the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board.
items.detail: Funds operations of the Board under chapter 21 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954. This is a stated authorization amount for fiscal year 2026.

items.main: Authorizes $13M for FY2026 naval petroleum reserve activities.
items.detail: Funds go to the Secretary of Energy for activities under chapter 869 of title 10, United States Code, relating to the naval petroleum reserves. The funds remain available until expended.

items.main: Authorizes $1.65B in FY2026 Maritime Administration and merchant marine appropriations (sum of the section's line items).
items.detail: Line items include $550M for the port infrastructure development program, $390M and $122.4M for U.S.-flag merchant marine national security support, $201.5M for the U.S. Merchant Marine Academy, $105.5M for Maritime Administration operations, $105M for small shipyards and training, $75M for the National Security Multi-Mission Vessel program, $59M for State maritime academies, $34M for the loan guarantee program, and $6M for obsolete vessel disposal.

items.main: Makes port infrastructure grants eligible to replace port cranes made or controlled by the People's Republic of China.
items.detail: Amends section 54301 of title 46 to add eligibility for projects that upgrade or replace port cranes, including hardware and software, that were installed or provided by, or are maintained, controlled, or sponsored by, the People's Republic of China or its instrumentalities.

items.main: Requires 100 percent U.S.-flag vessel transport for cargoes the Department of Transportation procures or finances.
items.detail: Amends section 55305 of title 46 to add an exception for the Department of Transportation: when it procures, contracts for, or finances equipment, materials, or commodities, 100 percent of the gross tonnage (computed separately for dry bulk carriers, dry cargo liners, and tankers) must move on privately owned U.S. commercial vessels, to the extent available at fair and reasonable rates.

items.main: $153.23B authorized for procurement across all services (House figure), up from the $152.83B request.
items.detail: Largest accounts are Shipbuilding and Conversion, Navy at $22.12B; Aircraft Procurement, Air Force at $17.94B; and Aircraft Procurement, Navy at $16.87B. Space Force procurement rises to $3.73B from a $3.39B request, largely from a $339.7M GPS III Follow-on add.

items.main: Shipbuilding funds two Columbia-class submarine lines and adds one DDG-51 destroyer.
items.detail: Columbia-class submarine is $3.93B plus $5.07B advance procurement; DDG-51 rises to $510.8M for one additional ship (+$500M); Virginia-class submarine rises to $1.82B (+$1.00B funding shortfall). A new Expeditionary Medical Ship line is $250M.

items.main: Strategic aircraft and missile lines include B-21 Raider and F-35.
items.detail: B-21 Raider is $2.59B plus $862.0M advance procurement; F-35 (Air Force) is $3.56B; National Security Space Launch is $1.47B. KC-46A is reduced to $2.50B (-$300M program delay).

sections.label: Title XLII — Research, Development, Test, and Evaluation

items.main: $142.44B authorized for research, development, test, and evaluation, up from the $142.00B request.
items.detail: By service (House figures): Air Force $53.08B; Defense-wide $33.48B; Navy $25.73B; Space Force $15.12B; Army $14.72B. Operational Test and Evaluation, Defense is $318.1M.

items.main: $295.08B authorized for operation and maintenance — the division's largest title.
items.detail: By component (House figures): Navy $73.97B; Air Force $62.13B; Army $59.19B; Defense-wide $55.60B. Reserve and National Guard components are authorized in separate lines.

items.main: $181.05B authorized for military personnel, reduced $750M from the $181.80B request.
items.detail: The reduction is attributed to historical unobligated balances. The MERHCF account is authorized at $12.85B.

items.main: $44.68B authorized for other authorizations, most of it the Defense Health Program.
items.detail: Defense Health Program is $41.00B, with In-House Care raised to $11.10B. Other lines include the Defense Commissary Agency working capital fund $1.53B, Drug Interdiction and Counter-Drug Activities $904.3M, and the DoD Inspector General $521.8M.

items.main: $18.89B authorized for military construction and family housing.
items.detail: The table lists projects by state, installation, and account; the total is $18.89B, unchanged from the request. It includes Base Realignment and Closure (BRAC) lines by service.

sections.label: Title XLVII — Department of Energy National Security Programs

items.main: $33.64B authorized for Atomic Energy Defense Activities at the Department of Energy.
items.detail: The National Nuclear Security Administration is $25.45B (Weapons Activities $20.58B; Defense Nuclear Nonproliferation $2.29B; Naval Reactors $2.03B). Defense Environmental Cleanup is $7.01B and Other Defense Activities is $1.18B.

sections.label: Title LI — Prohibitions Relating to Central Bank Digital Currency

items.main: Prohibits Federal Reserve banks from issuing a central bank digital currency and from offering retail banking directly to individuals.
items.detail: Amends section 16 of the Federal Reserve Act (12 U.S.C. 411) so a Federal reserve bank may not offer financial products or services directly to an individual, maintain an account on behalf of an individual, or issue a CBDC or substantially similar digital asset (Sec. 5102), and may not do so indirectly through a financial institution or other intermediary (Sec. 5103). Section 5101 cites the title as the “Anti-CBDC Surveillance State Act”.

items.main: Bars the Board of Governors from developing, creating, or using a CBDC and states it currently lacks authority to issue one.
items.detail: Amends section 10 of the Federal Reserve Act (12 U.S.C. 241) to prohibit the Board of Governors from testing, studying, developing, creating, or implementing a CBDC, and bars the Board and the Federal Open Market Committee from using a CBDC to implement monetary policy, with an exception for open, permissionless, and private dollar-denominated currency that preserves the privacy protections of physical currency (Sec. 5104). Section 5105 expresses the sense of Congress that the Federal Reserve currently has no authority to issue a CBDC and will not unless Congress grants it.

items.main: Reauthorizes Coast Guard appropriations for fiscal years 2025-2029, replacing the prior fiscal years 2022 and 2023 authorization.
items.detail: Amends 14 U.S.C. 4902 to set a first appropriation line at $11.29B (FY2025), $11.85B (FY2026), $13.50B (FY2027), $14.50B (FY2028), and $15.50B (FY2029); a second line at $3.63B (FY2025) rising to $3.80B (FY2029); and retired pay at $1.15B (FY2025) rising to $1.65B (FY2029). It also raises two sub-limits within the first line to $25.57M and $26.85M. Section 6101 cites the division as the “Coast Guard Authorization Act of 2025”.

underreported.summary: Grants the Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina federal recognition, eligibility for all federal tribal services, and land-into-trust authority.
underreported.why_unreported: Tribal recognition and land-into-trust authority placed in the Other Defense Matters subtitle of a defense authorization, unrelated to the defense subject matter of the title.

underreported.summary: Bars using a single-sex facility on a military installation that does not correspond to a person's sex, and defines male and female by reproductive biology.
underreported.why_unreported: A personnel access rule and statutory sex definitions carried inside the military-construction division.

underreported.summary: Cuts DoD discretionary budget authority by .5 percent for any fiscal year the Department has not obtained at least a qualified audit opinion, with the cut retained for deficit reduction.
underreported.why_unreported: An audit-enforcement funding penalty inside the general-provisions title rather than a stated audit reform.

underreported.summary: Prohibits the Federal Reserve from issuing a central bank digital currency and from offering retail accounts or products directly to individuals.
underreported.why_unreported: A Federal Reserve Act amendment on digital currency carried inside a national defense authorization act.

gaps: The policy divisions (A, B, C) authorize amounts 'as specified in' the Division D and section 4601/4701 funding tables, so the narrative titles state few aggregate dollar figures on their own.
The bill authorizes appropriations but does not itself appropriate funds; actual spending depends on later appropriations acts.
Division E bars the Federal Reserve from issuing a central bank digital currency but does not address digital-currency activity by other federal agencies or by private issuers beyond the Fed.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Houlahan
featured_quotes.text: I was very proud of the markup that passed out of the Armed Services Committee. The bill that we delivered to this floor this week was overwhelmingly bipartisan. It supported our men and women in uniform and strengthened our national defense. It was an honor to work so closely with Chairman Rogers and Ranking Member Smith on that bill. Unfortunately, the toxically amended bill that is here before us is no longer that.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Rogers
featured_quotes.text: I echo the ranking member's comments. This is a very bipartisan product that came out of committee. It is a good product, and it deserves this Chamber's support. He has been a great partner in fashioning what we bring to the floor today.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Jackson
featured_quotes.text: The Intelligence and Special Operations Subcommittee portions of this bill, in conjunction with approximately $2.2 billion in reconciliation funding, continues to focus on providing our Special Operations Forces, the Defense Intelligence Enterprise, and the security cooperation enterprise with the tools required to ensure their capabilities can support the Department's efforts in strategic competition and in countering malign PRC actions.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. McCormick
featured_quotes.text: I rise and offer my amendment No. 25 to H.R. 3838, the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026. My amendment expands on language already in law, in this bill, and in the Senate NDAA to combat the indirect censorship of conservative news outlets in the Department of War.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Rose
featured_quotes.text: My amendment is intended to address the Janet Mello fraud case, the Army civilian who was indicted and pleaded guilty to stealing over $100 million that were intended for the 4-H Military Partnership Grant Program. The 4-H Military Partnership Grant Program serves 4-H clubs that are in many military installation youth centers. These programs include 4-H positive youth development programming, engaging in hands-on learning in day and overnight summer camps, including military team adventure camps.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Stauber
featured_quotes.text: The first requires the Secretary of the Air Force and the Director of the Air National Guard to work together to modernize the Air National Guard's fighter fleet. Last year's NDAA required a similar report, but this report did not fulfill several requirements, like consultation from the Director of the Air National Guard and recapitalization plans for all fighter wings. It was entirely inadequate.

divisions.label: Division A — Department of Defense Authorizations
divisions.summary: Authorizes fiscal year 2026 programs, policy, and personnel levels for the Department of Defense across 18 titles — procurement, research, operation and maintenance, personnel policy and pay, military health care, acquisition reform, organization, foreign-nation matters, cyberspace, and space and strategic programs. It sets total active-duty strength at 1,302,800, overhauls defense acquisition (the SPEED Act), bars diversity, equity, and inclusion offices, and establishes the Golden Dome missile-defense program.
divisions.brief: Sets fiscal year 2026 Department of Defense authorizations and policy across 18 titles, including personnel end strengths, acquisition reform, and missile-defense programs.

subs: 1,302,800 active-duty personnel authorized for FY2026
Contract authority for up to 2 Ford carriers and 5 Columbia submarines
Air-refueling tanker floor raised from 466 to 504 aircraft
